data.analysis: Keep N=3 and all role identities. The supplied topics are distinct enough to retain: T1 validates all bytes with SIMD, T2 uses SIMD only to skip ASCII spans before scalar decoding, and T3 targets scalar decoding cost. T1/T2 still share the unverified assumptions that targeted SIMD is usable under the frozen build and that the scored mixed-width input has a distribution their methods benefit from. The baseline is already valid and measured at a mean 49.623 µs over three samples; there are no candidate results. Revisions sharpen the contrasts, ask the trees not to presume input composition or branch cost, and leave room to report useful hybrids. Any integrated program must be measured anew rather than assigned additive gains.

revisions.objective: Primary hypothesis: SIMD masks validate UTF-8 constraints across the whole buffer, unlike T2's ASCII-span locator. Explore block classification, shifted continuation requirements, restricted second-byte checks, cross-block state, and a bounded tail. Compare relevant SIMD variants only when supported by the frozen target and unchanged build; do not alter flags or add runtime environment probing. Keep the supplied scalar implementation as a control, and report any useful hybrid as a distinct variant rather than excluding it. Preserve exact scalar-value validation, ABI, output, and thread budget. Use the official mixed-width n=65536 timing for performance and official ASCII/malformed checks for correctness, paying particular attention to vector boundaries and truncations where covered. Record failed variants.
revisions.subject: Whole-stream SIMD UTF-8 validation with cross-block state

revisions.objective: Primary hypothesis: vector high-bit scans can skip ASCII spans while the existing strict scalar decoder handles non-ASCII code points. The benefit depends on the actual official mixed-width input containing useful ASCII spans; do not assume this or use synthetic-only results as evidence for the scored workload. Start decoding at a known code-point boundary and treat the first high-bit byte as input to validate—not as an assumed lead, since it may be a stray continuation. Keep loads and tails within n. Preserve exact validity, ABI, output, and thread budget. Measure the official mixed-width n=65536 workload and run the official ASCII/malformed correctness checks, especially for boundaries. Report this approach separately from T1's whole-buffer validation; label any hybrid distinctly and record failed variants.
revisions.subject: SIMD-assisted ASCII-run skipping with a scalar slow path

revisions.objective: Primary hypothesis: reducing scalar decoding control flow or dependencies helps the mixed-width workload; the supplied baseline already has an ASCII fast path, so do not assume ASCII scanning is the only scalar cost. Compare the baseline decoder with compact-state/DFA or reduced-branch scalar variants, measuring each under the official mixed-width n=65536 workload and checking official ASCII/malformed correctness. Keep scalar decoding as the focus, but do not treat that focus as a ban on useful correctness-preserving experiments; label any hybrid separately from pure-scalar results. Preserve exact validity, ABI, output, bounds, and thread budget. Report failed variants.
revisions.subject: Branch-reduced scalar UTF-8 decoding

data.shared_assumptions: Use the same frozen EPYC 9654/GCC 14.2 target, build, correctness/timing protocol, and single-core budget. The scored performance case is valid mixed-width n=65536; ASCII and malformed inputs are correctness checks. No measured input-composition details or child results are supplied. GCC target-attribute documentation describes a compilation mechanism, not proof of build flags or runtime feature availability. T1 and T2 overlap in SIMD machinery but test different work; any hybrid or final integration needs its own correctness validation and measurement.
